geography.guidance: Everywhere on the planet, the United States first (owner, 2026-09-09). An empty allowed list means every country except the disallowed set; the priority list earns the us_priority bonus and gets six searches in ten. Disallowed by design: Canada (CASL requires consent), Germany and Austria (UWG: consent for B2B email), Italy (consent). The connectors mark a lead 'disallowed' only on confirmed evidence -- a channel's country field, a feed's language REGION suffix (a bare language is not a country), Wikidata's country -- and blank always passes (Invariant 1).

languages.guidance: Clipping quality depends on editors understanding the content. English and Hindi are full credit; the partial list is where LCX can work with a native reviewer. Anything else scores 0 on language_match but is not gated out.

rubric.label: Deep back catalogue of long-form (100+ episodes or long videos)
rubric.guidance: 1.0 at 100+ long-form items, 0.5 at 40-99, 0 below 40. From the feed's episode count (Apple's trackCount when the feed is capped) or the channel's long-video count. The archive is the raw material; no archive, nothing to clip. LOWERED 2026-09-09 from 25 to 20 (see audience_band).

rubric.label: Publishes weekly or better and is active in the last 90 days
rubric.guidance: 1.0 at 4+ items a month over the last 90 days, 0.5 at 2-3 a month, 0 below. A show that still publishes needs clips every week; that is the retainer. LOWERED 2026-09-09 from 15 to 10 (see audience_band).

rubric.label: Shorts gap: long-form output with few or no shorts
rubric.guidance: 1.0 when under 10% of the last 50 uploads are shorts, 0.5 at 10-30%, 0 at 30%+ (they already clip). Only assessable when a YouTube channel is known -- for an audio-only podcast it stays unassessed, which is not evidence either way. This number IS the pitch: 'you have 214 episodes and 3 shorts'.

rubric.label: Audience in the band that can pay but has no in-house team (10k-1M subscribers)
rubric.guidance: 1.0 at 10k-1M subscribers, 0.5 at 3k-10k or 1M-3M, 0 outside. Below the band there is no budget; above it there is usually an editor on staff. Unassessed when no channel is known. RAISED 2026-09-09 from 15 to 25 after the first live run: catalogue and cadence alone let a 271-subscriber show outrank the band, and the audience is what decides whether there is a budget.

rubric.label: Evidence of a budget: sponsors, Patreon, merch, courses, a paid newsletter
rubric.guidance: Regex over the feed description and recent episode notes (or channel and video descriptions): sponsor reads, promo codes, Patreon, merch, membership, course, newsletter. 1.0 at two or more distinct signals, 0.5 at one, 0 when we looked and found none.

rubric.label: A business address to write to
rubric.guidance: Auto-set by the engine: 1.0 for an email the show published itself (feed owner address, not a hosting provider's), 0.5 for a website with a contact route, 0 for neither.

rubric.label: Content in a language LCX edits well
rubric.guidance: 1.0 for English or Hindi, 0.5 for the partial list, 0 otherwise. Small weight on purpose: it shapes the order, it does not veto.

score_modifiers.label: PENALTY: produced by a network or studio with its own post team
score_modifiers.guidance: 1.0 when the feed's author or owner is a known network (iHeart, Wondery, NPR, Spotify Studios and the like) or the channel is a media brand's. They have editors; the pitch is a different one. Soft subtractor; the biggest names are also hard-gated below.

score_modifiers.label: BONUS: the show is video-first on YouTube
score_modifiers.guidance: 1.0 when a YouTube channel with long-form uploads is confirmed. Video-native shows are the easiest to clip well and the quickest to see results.

score_modifiers.label: PENALTY: audience between 2M and 5M subscribers, probably staffed
score_modifiers.guidance: 1.0 when subscribers are above 2M (the gate takes over above 5M). Keeps big-but-not-huge channels in the pool, ranked below the band where the pitch lands.

score_modifiers.label: BONUS: based in the United States, the segment's first market
score_modifiers.guidance: 1.0 when the country is confirmed US (channel country, feed language region, Wikidata, or the TVF pool), 0 for any other confirmed country, absent when unknown. Eight points is enough to rank a US show above an otherwise identical one elsewhere, not enough to lift a weak lead into the band.

gates.label: Must not be in a country where cold business email is off limits
gates.guidance: Fires ONLY on confirmed evidence of a disallowed country (see geography.disallowed_countries). Blank/unknown always passes through.

gates.label: Show or channel must be currently active, not dormant
gates.guidance: Fires ONLY when the latest episode or upload is more than 180 days old. Blank/unknown always passes through.

gates.label: Not children's content or music
gates.guidance: Kids & Family (COPPA exposure, brand risk) and Music (licensing makes clips a liability) are out. Set from Apple genres or YouTube topic categories. Blank passes.

gates.label: Must have SOME way to be reached: email, website, or channel
gates.guidance: Fires only on an explicit false: no email, no website, no channel. Blank passes.

gates.label: Exclude the biggest podcast networks and broadcasters outright
gates.guidance: Name match against major_networks. These are not customers for a clipping desk; they are the competition's customers or have their own. Blank passes.

gates.label: Exclude channels far beyond the band (over 5M subscribers)
gates.guidance: First live run (2026-09-09): a 40M-subscriber gaming channel scored 92 because audience_band only withholds 15 points. Channels that size have a post team and a procurement process; they are not clipping customers. Set from the channel's subscriber count. Blank passes.

podcast_discovery.guidance: Apple's public podcast search needs no key and returns up to 200 shows per term and store country, with the feed URL and the episode count. The feed itself carries what we score on and the business address the show published on purpose. Terms are broad on purpose: the rubric, not the query, decides who ranks.

youtube_channel_discovery.guidance: A channel search costs 100 quota units, so a run does at most a few dozen searches; the channel statistics and the last 50 uploads cost 3 units per channel. The shorts gap, cadence and audience come straight from the API -- the pitch sentence is a fact. Long-form starts at eight minutes: a ten-minute explainer clips as well as an hour-long interview, and a twenty-minute floor threw away most education and commentary channels on the first live run (2026-09-09).

sources.name: Apple Podcasts search + the show's own RSS feed
sources.detail: tools/discover_podcasts.py -- keyless. Search terms x store countries -> feed URLs -> feed parsed for cadence, catalogue, monetization signals, YouTube link and the published contact.

sources.name: YouTube Data API v3 (channel search + statistics + last 50 uploads)
sources.detail: tools/discover_youtube_channels.py and the YouTube half of tools/enrich_clipping.py. Needs YOUTUBE_API_KEY. Shorts gap, cadence, audience, monetization hits.

sources.name: Wikidata production companies with a YouTube channel
sources.detail: tools/discover_wikidata_channels.py -- SPARQL per class, then the same 3-unit channel profile. Worldwide, US first. kind=production_house.

sources.name: TVF's US production-house pool, carried over with contacts
sources.detail: tools/import_pool.py --from us-production-houses. Name, website, contacts and origin; the enrichment pass finds the YouTube channel from the website.

self_exclusion.guidance: TVF and LCX properties never enter the pool. Same conservative matching as the TVF segment: exact host or subdomain, whole-word name patterns.

enrichment.guidance: The contact usually arrives with the discovery record (the feed's owner address). tools/enrich_clipping.py lifts it into contacts, adds YouTube evidence for shows with a channel, and computes the scoring inputs. The site-scrape pass (enrich_contacts) still runs for shows with a website and no address.

sender.name: LCX
sender.title: Clipping desk
sender.postal_address: SET_ME street address for the email footer (CAN-SPAM)
sender.guidance: The canonical sign-off a draft is stored in (name LCX, title Clipping desk, company LCX: it reads "LCX / Clipping desk, LCX", the same text as before 2026-10-13), never what goes out: since the owner's update of 2026-10-13 ("sign with the approver's name", sign_as approver) whoever opens a draft sees it signed with their own name and title, approving stores exactly that, and approval is refused while the approver's profile has no name or title. The name was SET_ME until then; it may not be, because SET_ME must never appear in a draft. The address is retained as an optional footer field and omitted from the email footer (owner, 2026-10-09); it stays SET_ME until the owner confirms one (2026-10-13: it is not in the footer, so it never reaches a draft, and `outreach.py send` refuses this project while it is SET_ME). The sending address is the project's own pool mailbox (mailboxes).

outreach.sign_as_guidance: The owner, 2026-10-13: "sign with the approver's name". LCX Clipping keeps sending from its own pool mailboxes (mailboxes, not send_from approver), but each email is signed with the approving person's own name and title, as LCX Services' emails are (tools/draft_render.signs_as_approver, personalize; app/main.py approval).
outreach.subject_max_words_guidance: The owner, 2026-10-13: "subject for all emails for all services should be less than 5 or equal to 5 words". Every rendered subject is checked against this (tools/draft_render.capped_subject): one over it uses its template's subject_fallback, and one still over it is not drafted, so a longer subject never ships. "Re:" in front of a follow-up is not counted. A follow-up repeats its opener's subject to stay in its Gmail thread, so it has no fallback of its own: one whose opener's subject is over the cap is not drafted.

send_window.guidance: Owner, 2026-10-12: "I want you to send mails to the sender's time region between 10 to 10:30AM and that must be randmized not like all mail going at 10:15 some must be going at 10:17 some at 10:13 and so on after approval implement it". Each approved email goes out at its own random second between start and end on its RECIPIENT's clock (10:00 in Mumbai is 05:30 in London, too early to be read), drawn when it is approved and shown in Approved as "Goes out", with the time in India beside it. Where the recipient is comes from what the lead holds -- the person's own Apollo record, the company's state or city, a phone's area code, its country -- and the reason is kept on the email (tools/send_window.py). Monday to Friday on the recipient's clock (weekdays_only): an approval after today's window, or at a weekend, takes the next weekday's. An email whose window passes unsent (the server down, its address at its daily limit) moves to the next window at a new random time, never later the same day. Never two emails from one address closer than min_gap_seconds; never one sooner than min_lead_seconds after its approval. To send on the sender's clock instead (every email 10:00-10:30 India time) set timezone_of to "sender"; to switch the window off set enabled to false -- the stored times are cleared and approvals go out as soon as they can, as before. docs/runbook.md, "Goes out". Sending is paused for this project (sending_paused); the window applies from the day it is lifted. A show that names no place goes at New York's 10:00 (fallback_timezone).

outreach.neutral_hook: We've been mapping shows with a deep back catalogue and almost no short-form, and {{company}} came up.

templates.subject: Your episodes, as shorts
templates.guidance: First touch for creators and podcasters. {{hook}} is one sentence of THEIR numbers -- episodes, cadence, length, shorts count -- built by the draft command from the feed and channel evidence, so it is true by construction. Greeting: a person's first name when the engine found one (metadata.host at high or medium confidence); otherwise 'there'. Never the show's name.

templates.subject: Shorts from your archive
templates.guidance: Production houses and studios (metadata.kind = production_house, set by the Wikidata connector and the TVF pool import). Same evidence hook, studio wording: 'your archive', 'your team approves'. Picked automatically by the draft command through the `when` condition.

templates.subject: Re: {{opener_subject}}
templates.guidance: Follow-up 1, sent in the opener's thread four days after it if nobody replied. Short on purpose.

templates.subject: Re: {{opener_subject}}
templates.guidance: Follow-up 2, the last one: seven days after follow-up 1. After this the thread is closed for good.

outreach.guidance: Everything outbound is drafted -> human-approved -> sent, in that order. Approval may be one draft at a time or a spot-checked batch (batch_approval). daily_send_cap is a hard daily ceiling per mailbox and counts follow-ups. One thread per company, enforced by the database: an opener, then at most the follow_ups steps, stopped by any reply. Templates carry an optional `when` condition on metadata; follow-up templates are marked kind=follow_up and are never used as openers. greeting_fallback is what 'Hi ...' says when no person is known. Subjects (owner, 2026-10-13): at most subject_max_words, with no company name. The footer -- the sign-off -- is one setting for the whole segment (outreach.footer.text), edited in the app under Outreach -> Footer; templates end with {{footer}}.

follow_ups.guidance: Owner decision 2026-09-10. One thread per company: the opener plus these steps, in the same Gmail thread, each counted from the previous email's send. Any reply pauses the thread at once; a reply triaged as an auto-reply lets it resume, anything else ends it. A person can stop a thread from the message dialog. Follow-ups are drafts and need approval like any email. The database caps a thread at three follow-ups and refuses to send one after a reply (sql/23).

batch_approval.guidance: Owner decision 2026-09-10. Templated drafts may be approved together: select them in Drafts, read the random sample the server draws (at least sample_min, or sample_fraction of the batch, whichever is more), tick each, approve. Every draft is checked first (no {{placeholder}}, no SET_ME, a valid address, a sendable company). The approver's name, the batch and the sample are recorded.
batch_approval.generated_guidance: A spot check stands for a batch because every draft in it came from one template. A model-written sentence can be wrong on its own, so those drafts are approved one at a time. Set allow_generated to true once you have read enough of them to trust it; batches containing them then draw generated_sample_fraction instead of sample_fraction.

outreach.mailbox_guidance: Owner decision 2026-09-10. Openers are spread across the connected mailboxes, each to the one with the most room left today; follow-ups always leave from the mailbox that sent the opener (sql/24 enforces it). A mailbox takes part once its address is in .env under email_env and `outreach.py auth --mailbox <key>` has been run on the sending machine; the others are skipped, never guessed. Warm-up: start_cap a day from the mailbox's first send, +step every every_days, up to daily_cap (10 -> 40 over twelve days). Use addresses on a sending domain of LCX's own, not the main company domain, so a bad week cannot hurt everyday mail. Each email is signed by the person who approved it (sign_as approver, owner 2026-10-13), whichever mailbox it leaves from. daily_send_cap is the ceiling across all of them.

footer.guidance: Owner decision 2026-10-09: the sign-off, with the postal address omitted. The owner, 2026-10-13: the opt-out line is removed from every project's footer ("remove the last line from every single service"); any reply that is not neutral still stops all mail to that address. The name and title are the approver's own (sign_as approver); since 2026-10-13 the title line reads "<title>, LCX" with the company from sender.company, as LCX Services' does, so a person's own title never reads as if the clipping desk were theirs. Edited in Outreach -> Footer. Postal addresses are optional; templates end with {{footer}}.

generated_hook.guidance: The opening sentence of a draft, written by a model from the facts whitelist in tools/draft_render.facts_for(): public counts grouped by what each one measures, never an address, a contact name, page text, a URL, the channel country or an episode title. Every number the model writes must appear in those facts or the sentence is thrown away and the deterministic hook is used instead; so is anything with no number at all, a link, markup, emoji, a sales or proportion word, an average stated as a length, or more than two sentences. A lead with no counts is not sent. No GROQ_API_KEY means no calls and no change. The sentence is stored on the outreach row, so what a person approved is what is sent. See tools/llm.py and docs/LCX_clipping.md.

wikidata_channel_discovery.guidance: tools/discover_wikidata_channels.py. Direct instances of each class that list a YouTube channel (P2397), with website (P856) and country (P17 -> ISO). One query per class; subclass walks time out. Priority countries are profiled first. Floors are lower than for creators because a production house with a modest channel and a deep archive is still a clipping customer.

auto_shortlist.guidance: Owner decision 2026-09-14. Every ready_for_review lead with fit_score strictly above min_score is shortlisted by the last step of the promote chain (sql/14_auto_shortlist.sql) instead of by hand. Rejected, archived and contacted rows are never touched, and a lead a person moves back to review is never shortlisted again (metadata.auto_shortlisted_at). Shortlisting sends nothing: every draft still needs approval. Set enabled to false to go back to shortlisting by hand.
